newsitem.title: KENYA: FOCUS - Kenya shilling falls as violence erupts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Kenya shilling falls as violence erupts.

text.p: The Kenyan shilling took a further beating on Thursday, driven down by panic-triggered demand for dollars after the worst political violence since pluralist politics returned in 1991.
Commercial bank dealers said even intervention central bank intervention could not stem a weakening shilling.
The central bank posted a mean shilling rate of 56.38 against the dollar from 55.87 on Wednesday. Against the pound, the shilling was posted at a mean of 95.10 from 94.26.
Dealers said the shilling slipped to 56.80/57.80 in the morning session from an opening of 56.17/56.59.
"There was some intervention by central bank, about five million dollars, trying to add some liquidity in the market. But it didn't do enough," one dealer said.
"The market is very jittery. Spreads are very wide. Everyone's quoting very cautiously because dollars are being taken at almost any price," a senior dealer from a leading commercial bank said.

Kenya, East Africa's economic engine and usually an oasis of stability, saw opposition groups, backed by churches and university students, demanding sweeping constitutional reforms before presidential and parliamentary elections later this year.
Some nine people were killed at the height of violence on Monday, and the unrest is getting investors and business concerns running scared.
On Wednesday, central bank Governor Micah Cheserem said the shilling had taken a beating due to market jitters following Monday's unrest but that the phenomenon was temporary.
Although the panic appeared temporary, dealers said sustained central bank intervention was necessary to protect the currency from falling more amid very thin supply.
"The central bank needs to pump in more dollars to stabilise the shilling. Then, at least people will see there is no need to pay desperate prices for dollars," one dealer said.
The money market was tight. Overnight rates were quoted at 23 percent from 17-22 percent on Thursday.

Economists said the currency and the general economy would suffer greatly unless the country's political managers showed it could rein in the violence and rekindle fast evaporating investor and business confidence.
The opposition wants sweeping reforms before elections later this year, but President Daniel arap Moi, instead, promised reforms only after the polls.
